column2: embodied rivers and the eternal Vedas, oceans and lakes and various tirthas, the Earth, the Sky, the quarters and the trees, lord of men,
Aditi, mother of the gods, Hri, Shri, Svaha, Sarasvati, Uma, Shachi, Sinivali, Anumati, Kuhu, Raka and Dhishana, and the other wives of the dwellers in heaven,
the Himalaya and the Vindhya, Meru with his many peaks, Airavata with his followers, the kalas and kashthas (divisions of time), the half-months, months and seasons, nights and days, O king,
Uchchaihshravas, best of horses, Vamana the king of serpents, Aruna and Garuda, and the trees with the herbs,
and the revered god Dharma—all came together, with Time, Yama, Death and Yama's attendants.
And the various hosts of gods not named for their multitude came from here and there for the Kumara's consecration.
Then, O king, all those dwellers in heaven took the vessel for the consecration and all auspicious things.
With golden pitchers furnished with divine materials, O king, and with the holy waters of the Sarasvatis, divine waters,
the delighted dwellers in heaven consecrated the Kumara as general, the great soul, a terror to the asuras.
As in former times, great king, the revered Brahma, Grandsire of the worlds, consecrated Varuna as lord of the waters, so too did Kashyapa of great splendour and others not mentioned.
To him Brahma, pleased, gave mighty attendants, swift as the wind, perfected ones who bear power at will, great retainers.
Nandishena, Lohitaksha, Ghantakarna, and the fourth, his renowned attendant Kumudamalin.
Then Sthanu (Shiva), O king of kings, gave to Skanda, destroyer of the foes of the gods, a swift great retainer, Kratu, holder of hundreds of illusions, Kama, endowed with strength and power at will.
In the war of gods and asuras, enraged, he slew with his arms fourteen myriads of the Daityas of dreadful deeds.
Likewise the gods gave him an army thronged with Rakshasas, destroying the enemies of the gods, invincible and of every form.
Then all the gods with Vasava raised the cry of victory, and Gandharvas, Yakshas, Rakshasas, sages and ancestors.
Yama gave two attendants like Yama and Kala, Unmatha and Pramatha, of great valour and great splendour.
Subhraja and Bhaskara, the two followers of the Sun—these the mighty Sun, pleased, gave to Karttikeya.
Like peaks of Kailasa, wearing white garlands and unguents, Soma also gave two attendants, Mani and Sumani.
Fire gave to his son Jvalajihva and Jyoti, two heroic attendants who crush enemy armies.
Amsha too gave the wise Skanda five attendants: Parigha, Vata, the exceedingly mighty Bhima, and Dahati and Dahana, both fierce and esteemed for valour.
Vasava, slayer of heroes, gave Fire's son Utkrosha and Pankaja, both bearers of thunderbolt-clubs, who slew many of Mahendra's enemies in battle.
Vishnu of great renown gave Skanda three attendants: Chakra, Vikramaka and the mighty Sankramaka.
The Ashvins, pleased, gave Skanda Vardhana and Nandana, both skilled in all sciences, bull of the Bharatas.
Dhata gave the great soul Kundana, Kusuma, Kumuda, and the renowned Dambara and Adambara.
Tvashta gave the great soul Skanda the excellent attendants Vakra and Anuvakra, mighty, ram-faced, and strong, masters of great illusion.
Mitra gave the great soul Kumara the great souls Suvrata and Satyasandha, bearers of austerity and knowledge.
Vidhata gave Karttikeya the handsome boon-givers, renowned in the three worlds, the great soul Suprabha and Shubhakarma.
Pushan gave Karttikeya two attendants, Palitaka and Kalika, both great masters of illusion, Bharata.
Vayu gave Karttikeya Bala and Atibala, of great faces and great strength, best of the Bharatas.
Varuna, true to his pledge, gave Karttikeya Ghasa and Atighasa, of whale-like faces and great strength.
The Himalaya gave, O king, the great souls Suvarchas and Ativarchas to Fire's son.
Meru gave Fire's son two attendants, the great soul Kanchana and Meghamalin, Bharata.
Meru also gave the great-souled son of Fire two others, Sthira and Atisthira, of great strength and valour.
The Vindhya gave Fire's son two attendants, Uchchhrita and Atishringa, who fight with great boulders.
The ocean gave Fire's son two mace-bearing great attendants, Samgraha and Vigraha.
The fair-looking Parvati gave Fire's son Unmada, Pushpadanta and Shankukarna.
Vasuki, lord of serpents, tiger among men, gave Fire's son two serpents, Jaya and Mahajaya.
Thus the Sadhyas, Rudras, Vasus, ancestors, oceans, rivers and mighty mountains
gave him leaders of the host, bearing spears and pattishas, furnished with divine weapons and adorned in many guises.

Some had tortoise and cock faces, hare and owl faces, ass and camel faces, and boar faces,
human and ram faces, jackal faces, dreadful crocodile faces and dolphin faces,
cat and hare faces, long faces, Bharata, mongoose and owl faces, and others with dog faces,
rat and mongoose faces, peacock faces, fish and ram faces, others with goat, sheep and buffalo faces,
bear and tiger faces, leopard and lion faces, dreadful elephant faces, and others with crocodile faces,
Garuda faces, rhinoceros faces, wolf and crow faces, others with cow, ass and camel faces, and gadfly faces,
with great bellies, feet and limbs, Bharata, star-eyed, others with pigeon faces and others with bull faces,
others with cuckoo faces, hawk and partridge faces, lizard faces, clad in spotless garments of the sky,
serpent-faced, spear-faced, fierce-faced, hundred-faced, venomous serpents, bark-clad, with cow-nose coverings,
big-bellied and thin-limbed, big-limbed and thin-bellied, short-necked, big-eared, adorned with many serpents,
clad in the hide of the best of elephants, and in black antelope skins, with faces on the shoulders, O great king, and faces on the belly,
faces on the back, jaw-faced, faces on the calves, many with faces on the sides, with faces of various lands,
lords of hosts with faces like insects and moths, others with the faces of many serpents, bearing many arms and heads,
some with arms like various trees, others with heads at the waist, with faces like serpent-coils, dwelling in various thickets,
with bodies wrapped in bark and robed in plank-cloth, wearing various garbs and clad in hides,
turbaned, crowned, conch-necked, radiant, diadem-wearing, five-crested, with stiff hair,
three-crested and two-crested, others seven-crested, peacock-crested, crowned, shaven and matted,
some wearing wondrous garlands, some with hairy faces, wearing divine garlands and garments, ever pleasing in form,
black, with fleshless faces, long-backed, bellyless, thick-backed, short-backed, with hanging bellies and organs,
long-armed, short-armed, short-bodied, dwarfish, hunchbacked, long-shanked, with elephant ears and necks,
elephant-nosed, tortoise-nosed, wolf-nosed, others long-lipped, long-tongued, frightful, with downturned faces,
with great tusks, short tusks, four tusks, and others like lordly elephants, dreadful, O king, in their thousands,
well-proportioned in body, radiant, well adorned, tawny-eyed, spike-eared and crooked-nosed, Bharata,
broad-tusked, great-tusked, thick-lipped, green-haired, with various feet, lips and tusks, with various arms and heads, covered in various armours and speaking various tongues, Bharata,
skilled in the languages of regions, speaking to one another, the lords and great retainers rushed about in joy.
Long-necked, long-nailed, with long feet, heads and arms, tawny-eyed, blue-throated and long-eared, Bharata,
some like wolf-bellied, some like collyrium, white-limbed, red-necked, tawny-eyed, others dappled, many variegated in colour, O king, Bharata,
like chowries, white and red in streaks, of many colours and of single colours, with lustre like peacocks.
Again hear from me the weapons of these as I name them, the weapons taken up by the remaining retainers.
Some had nooses raised in their hands, open-mouthed, ass-faced, broad-eyed, blue-throated, with arms like iron bars,
hands holding shataghnis and discuses, and pestles, others with spear and sword in hand, huge-bodied and mighty.
With maces and bhushundis in hand, others with lances, with swords, clubs and staves in hand, Bharata.
With various dreadful weapons, great souls, of great speed, great strength and great force, the great retainers.
Seeing the Kumara's consecration, delighted, fond of battle, with their bodies wrapped in nets of bells, those greatly energetic ones danced.
These and many other great retainers, O king, attended the great-souled, renowned Karttikeya.
Divine, aerial and earthly heroes like the wind, assigned by the gods, became Skanda's attendants.
Thousands, myriads and hundreds of millions of such stood surrounding the consecrated great soul.
Hear, Bharata, the names of the glorious Mothers, by whom, auspicious, the three worlds, moving and unmoving, are pervaded.

Chatushpatharata, Bhuritirtha, Anyagochara, Pashuda, Vittada, Sukhada, Mahayashas, Payoda, Gomahishada and Suvishana, Bharata,

These and many other Mothers, bull of the Bharatas, followed Karttikeya, in thousands, of many forms.
Long-nailed, long-toothed, long-snouted, Bharata, some simple and sweet, in youth, well adorned,
endowed with greatness, taking forms at will, some fleshless-bodied, some white, some like gold,
others like black clouds, some smoke-coloured, bull of the Bharatas, some of ruddy hue, greatly fortunate, long-haired, white-clad,
with hair bound upward, tawny-eyed, with hanging girdles, big-bellied, long-eared and with hanging breasts,
copper-eyed, copper-hued, others tawny-eyed, boon-givers, roaming at will, ever cheerful.
Some of Yama's, of Rudra's, others gentle, of Kubera's, others of great strength, of Varuna, of Mahendra, and of Agni, scorcher of foes,
of Vayu, of Kumara and of Brahma, bull of the Bharatas; in beauty equal to Apsarases, in speed like the wind,
in speech like the cuckoo, in wealth like the giver of wealth, in vigour like Shakra, and in splendour like fire.
Dwelling in trees and crossroads, abiding at four-way junctions, living in caves and cremation grounds and mountain springs,
wearing various ornaments, various garlands and garments, of many wondrous guises and of many tongues,
these and many other hosts, terrifying to foes, followed the great soul with the approval of the lord of the gods.
Then the revered Pakashasana (Indra) gave Guha, tiger among kings, a spear-weapon for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
A banner, loud-sounding, with a great bell, shining, bright-lustred, of the colour of the young sun, Bharata,
Pashupati (Shiva) gave him, a great army of all beings, fierce, with various weapons, endowed with austerity, valour and strength.
Vishnu gave the Vaijayanti garland, which increases strength; Uma gave two spotless garments bright as the sun.
Ganga gave a divine, excellent water-pot born of nectar; Brihaspati, in affection, gave the Kumara a staff.
Garuda gave his beloved son, a peacock with variegated tail; Aruna gave a copper-crested cock, a weapon of the feet.
King Varuna gave a noose endowed with strength and valour; Brahma gave a black antelope skin to the one devoted to Brahmanas, and the creator of the worlds also gave victory in battles.
Having obtained generalship of the host of gods, Skanda shone, blazing, flaming, like a second Fire, accompanied by the retainers and the Mothers.
That army, Rakshasa-thronged and dreadful, with raised banners and bells, with kettledrums, conches and drums, with weapons and flags, shone like the autumn sky adorned with stars.
Then those hosts of gods and the troops of spirits undisturbed sounded kettledrums and many conches,
drums, jharjharas, krakachas, cow-horns, adambaras, gomukhas and loud-sounding dindimas.
All the gods with Vasava praised the Kumara, and divine Gandharvas sang and hosts of Apsarases danced.
Then, pleased, Mahasena gave the gods a boon: "I shall slay in battle the foes who wish to slay you."
Having received the boon from that best of the wise, the gods, great souls, glad at heart, thought their foes already slain.
A cry of joy rose from all the hosts of beings; when the boon was given by the great soul, it filled the three worlds.
Mahasena set out, surrounded by a great army, to slay the Daityas in battle and to protect the dwellers in heaven.
Resolve, Victory, Dharma, Success, Lakshmi, Steadfastness and Memory went in front of Mahasena's troops, O king.
Guha went forth, roaring, with that dreadful army, with spears and clubs in hand, with maces, pestles, iron arrows, spears and lances in hand, roaring like a proud lion.
Seeing him, all the Daityas, Rakshasas and Danavas fled in all directions on every side, disturbed by fear, and the gods pursued them with various weapons in hand.
Seeing this, Skanda, enraged, endowed with splendour and strength, the revered one, hurled the dreadful spear-weapon again and again, drawing in his own energy like a fire fed with oblations.
As the spear-weapon was hurled by Skanda of immeasurable splendour, flaming meteors, great king, fell to the ground.
Thunderbolts too fell roaring on the earth, as dreadful as at the time of the end of the age, O king.
When one spear was hurled by the dreadful son of Fire, crores of spears flew forth, bull of the Bharatas.
With that spear-weapon in the battle the revered lord slew the Daitya king named Taraka, of great strength and valour, surrounded by ten myriads of mighty Daitya heroes.
He also slew Mahisha in battle, surrounded by eight padmas; and he slew Tripada, surrounded by ten hundred myriads.
The lord slew Hradodara, surrounded by ten nikharvas, along with his followers bearing various weapons.
There, as the foes were being slain, the Kumara's attendants raised a vast roar, filling the ten quarters.
By the flames of the spear-weapon, O king of kings, and by Skanda's roars, thousands of Daityas were burned on every side, and others slain.
Some enemies of the gods were struck down by his banner, some, terrified by the sound of the bell, fell to the ground; some, cut by weapons, fell lifeless.
Thus the mighty hero Karttikeya in battle slew many violent enemies of the gods.
Then the Daitya named Bana, mighty son of Bali, reached Mount Krauncha and harassed the hosts of gods.
Mahasena, of noble mind, advanced against that enemy of the gods, who from fear of Karttikeya took refuge in Krauncha.
He cut off the wings of some and the heads of others, and the one whose weapon was his feet broke the legs of some.
When Yama drags off the brave and the fearful alike, Bharata, why then should those kshatriyas, bulls among kshatriyas, not fight?
When I used to hear his harsh and bitter words, spoken in the assembly at the dice-game for Duryodhana's benefit,
[The serpent said:] "Where there is no effect there is no action; even where the cause is absent, truth remains; therefore, concerning this cause, you should name the cause specially to me."
How can you, knower of all dharmas, skilled in all scriptures, again fall into delusion, Bharata, as though from ignorance?
Whatever Gandhari, the renowned, said, small or great, King Dhritarashtra did it.
While auspicious-day blessings were being uttered and the great souls were reciting prayers, running footsteps were heard, but no one was seen.
Then Fire, best of the Bharatas, vanished right there, and the heroic Pandavas went on, facing south.
The divine messenger went in front and the king behind, along an evil, difficult road frequented by evildoers.
